A-11 A P P E N D I X II Complex Functions ” The shortest path between two truths in the real domain passes through the complex domain. ” Jacques Hadamard 1865-1963 quoted in The Mathematical Intelligencer, v 13, 1991 Most of this book is concerned with developing the properties of real functions, that is, functions of one or more real variables, having values that are themselves real numbers or vectors with real components. The definition of function given in Section P.4 can be paraphrased to allow for complex-valued functions of a complex variable. D E F I N I T I O N 1 A complex function f is a rule that assigns a unique complex number f .z/ to each number z in some set of complex numbers (called the domain of the function). Typically, we will use z D x C yi to denote a general point in the domain of a complex function and w D uCvi to denote the value of the function at z; if w D f .z/, then the real and imaginary parts of w (u D Re .w/ and v D Im .w/) are real-valued functions of z, and hence real-valued functions of the two real variables x and y: u D u.x; y/; v D v.x; y/: For example, the complex function f .z/ D z2, whose domain is the whole complex plane C, assigns the value z2 to the complex number z. If w D z2 (where w D u C vi and z D x C yi), then u C vi D .x C yi/2 D x2 � y2 C 2xyi; so that u D Re .z2/ D x2 � y2 and v D Im .z2/ D 2xy: It is not convenient to draw the graph of a complex function. The graph of w D f .z/ would have to be drawn in a four-dimensional (real) space, since two dimen- sions (a z-plane) are required for the independent variable, and two more dimensions (a w-plane) are required for the dependent variable. Instead, we can graphically rep- resent the behaviour of a complex function w D f .z/ by drawing the z-plane and the w-plane separately, and showing the image in the w-plane of certain, appropriately chosen sets of points in the z-plane. For example, Figure II.1 illustrates the fact that for the function w D z2 the image of the quarter-disk jzj  a, 0  arg .z/   2 is the half-disk jwj  a2, 0  arg .w/  . APPENDIX II Complex Functions A-13 The Complex Derivative The definition of derivative is the same as for real functions: D E F I N I T I O N 4 The complex function f is differentiable at z and has derivative f 0.z/ there, provided lim h!0 f .z C h/ � f .z/ h D f 0.z/ exists. Note, however, that in this definition h is a complex number. The limit must exist no matter how h approaches 0 in the complex plane. This fact has profound implications. The existence of a derivative in this sense forces the function f to be much better behaved than is necessary for a differentiable real function. For example, it can be shown that if f 0.z/ exists for all z in an open region D in C, then f has derivatives of all orders throughout D: Moreover, such a function is the sum of its Taylor series f .z/ D f .z0/ C f 0.z0/.z � z0/ C f 00.z0/ 2Š .z � z0/2 C    about any point z0 in DI the series has positive radius of convergence R and converges in the disk jz � z0j < R. For this reason, complex functions that are differentiable on open sets in C are usually called analytic functions. It is beyond the scope of this introductory appendix to prove these assertions. They are proved in courses and texts on complex analysis. APPENDIX II Complex Functions A-17 The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra As observed at the beginning of Appendix I, extending the number system to include complex numbers allows larger classes of equations to have solutions. We conclude this appendix by verifying that polynomial equations always have solutions in the com- plex numbers. A complex polynomial of degree n is a function of the form Pn.z/ D anzn C an�1zn�1 C    C a2z2 C a1z C a0; where a0, a1, : : : , an are complex numbers and an ¤ 0. The numbers ai (0  i  n) are called the coefficients of the polynomial. If they are all real numbers, then Pn.x/ is called a real polynomial. A complex number z0 that satisfies the equation P .z0/ D 0 is called a zero or root of the polynomial. Every polynomial of degree 1 has a zero: if a1 ¤ 0, then a1z C a0 has zero z D �a0=a1. This zero is real if a1 and a0 are both real. Similarly, every complex polynomial of degree 2 has two zeros. If the polynomial is given by P2.z/ D a2z2 C a1z C a0 (where a2 ¤ 0), then the zeros are given by the quadratic formula z D z1 D �a1 � q a2 1 � 4a2a0 2a2 and z D z2 D �a1 C q a2 1 � 4a2a0 2a2 : In this case, P2.z/ has two linear factors: P2.z/ D a2.z � z1/.z � z2/: Even if a2 1 � 4a2a0 D 0, so that z1 D z2, we still regard the polynomial as having two (equal) zeros, one corresponding to each factor. A-18 APPENDIX II Complex Functions PROOF (We will only give an informal sketch of the proof.) We can assume that the coefficient of zn in P .z/ is an D 1, since we can divide the equation P .z/ D 0 by an without changing its solutions. We can also assume that a0 ¤ 0; if a0 D 0, then z D 0 is certainly a zero of P .z/. Thus, we deal with the polynomial P .z/ D zn C Q.z/; where Q.z/ is a polynomial of degree less than n having a nonzero constant term. If R is sufficiently large, then jQ.z/j will be less than Rn for all numbers z satisfying jzj D R. As z moves around the circle jzj D R in the z-plane, w D zn moves around the circle jwj D Rn in the w-plane (n times). Since the distance from zn to P .z/ is equal to jP .z/ � znj D jQ.z/j < Rn, it follows that the image of the circle jzj D R under the transformation w D P .z/ is a curve that winds around the origin n times. (If you walk around a circle of radius r n times, with your dog on a leash of length less than r, and your dog returns to his starting point, then he must also go around the centre of the circle n times.) This situation is illustrated for the particular case P .z/ D z3 C z2 � iz C 1; jzj D 2 in Figure II.3. The image of jzj D 2 is the large curve in the w-plane that winds around the origin three times. As R decreases, the curve traced out by w D P .z/ for jzj D R changes continuously. For R close to 0, it is a small curve staying close to the constant term a0 of P .z/. For small enough R the curve will not enclose the origin. (In Figure II.3 the image of jzj D 0:3 is the small curve staying close to the point 1 in the w-plane.) Thus, for some value of R, say R D R1, the curve must pass through the origin. That is, there must be a complex number z1, with jz1j D R1, such that P .z1/ D 0. A-21 A P P E N D I X III Continuous Functions ” Geometry may sometimes appear to take the lead over analysis, but in fact precedes it only as a servant goes before his master to clear the path and light him on the way. The interval between the two is as wide as between empiricism and science, as between the understanding and the reason, or as between the finite and the infinite. ” J. J. Sylvester 1814-1897 from Philosophic Magazine, 1866 The development of calculus depends in an essential way on the concept of the limit of a function and thereby on properties of the real number system. In Chapter 1 we presented these notions in an intuitive way and did not attempt to prove them except in Section 1.5, where the formal definition of limit was given and used to verify some elementary limits and prove some simple properties of limits. Many of the results on limits and continuity of functions stated in Chapter 1 may seem quite obvious; most students and users of calculus are not bothered by applying them without proof. Nevertheless, mathematics is a highly logical and rigorous dis- cipline, and any statement, however obvious, that cannot be proved by strictly logical arguments from acceptable assumptions must be considered suspect. In this appendix we build upon the formal definition of limit given in Section 1.5 and combine it with the notion of completeness of the real number system first encountered in Section P.1 to give formal proofs of the very important results about continuous functions stated in Theorems 8 and 9 of Section 1.4, the Max-Min Theorem and the Intermediate-Value Theorem. Most of our development of calculus in this book depends essentially on these two theorems. The branch of mathematics that deals with proofs such as these is called mathe- matical analysis. This subject is usually not pursued by students in introductory cal- culus courses but is postponed to higher years and studied by students in majors or honours programs in mathematics. It is hoped that some of this material will be of value to honours-level calculus courses and individual students with a deeper interest in understanding calculus. Limits of Functions At the heart of mathematical analysis is the formal definition of limit, Definition 8 in Section 1.5, which we restate as follows: The formal definition of limit We say that limx!a f .x/ D L if for every positive number  there exists a positive number ı, depending on  (i.e., ı D ı./), such that 0 < jx � aj < ı / jf .x/ � Lj < : Section 1.5 was marked “optional” because understanding the material presented there was not essential for learning calculus. However, that material is an essential prerequisite for this appendix. It is highly recommended that you go back to

These exercises provide proofs for the standard laws of limits stated in Section 1.2. Continuous Functions Consider the following definitions of continuity, which are equivalent to those given in Section 1.4. D E F I N I T I O N 1 Continuity of a function at a point A function f; defined on an open interval containing the point a, is said to be continuous at the point a if lim x!a f .x/ D f .a/I that is, if for every  > 0 there exists ı > 0 such that if jx � aj < ı, then jf .x/ � f .a/j < . D E F I N I T I O N 2 Continuity of a function on an interval A function f is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of that interval. Completeness and Sequential Limits D E F I N I T I O N 3 A real number u is said to be an upper bound for a nonempty set S of real numbers if x  u for every x in S. The number u is called the least upper bound or supremum of S if u is an upper bound for S and u  u for every upper bound u of S. The supremum of S is usually denoted sup.S/. Similarly, is a lower bound for S if  x for every x in S. The number  is the greatest lower bound or infimum of S if  is a lower bound for S and  for every lower bound of S. The infimum of S is denoted inf.S/. E X A M P L E 1 Set S1 D Œ2; 3 and S2 D .2; 1/. Any number u  3 is an upper bound for S1. S2 has no upper bound; we say that it is not bounded above. The least upper bound of S1 is sup.S1/ D 3. Any real number  2 is a lower bound for both S1 and S2. The greatest lower bound of each set is 2: inf.S1/ D inf.S2/ D 2. Note that the least upper bound and greatest lower bound of a set may or may not belong to that set. We now recall the completeness axiom for the real number system, which we discussed briefly in Section P.1. The completeness axiom for the real numbers A nonempty set of real numbers that has an upper bound must have a least upper bound. Equivalently, a nonempty set of real numbers having a lower bound must have a greatest lower bound. We stress that this is an axiom to be assumed without proof. It cannot be deduced from the more elementary algebraic and order properties of the real numbers. These other properties are shared by the rational numbers, a set that is not complete. The

A-33 A P P E N D I X V Doing Calculus with Maple ” I think, therefore I am. ” Rene´ Descartes 1596-1650 Discourse on Method ” AI [Artificial Intelligences] think, therefore I am. ” David Braue APC Magazine, November 2003 Computer algebra systems like Maple and Mathematica are capable of doing most of the tedious calculations involved in doing calculus, especially the very intensive calcu- lations required by many applied problems. (They cannot, of course, do the thinking for you; you must still fully understand what you are doing and what the limitations are of such programs.) Throughout this text we have inserted material illustrating how to use Maple to do common calculus-oriented calculations. These insertions range in length from single paragraphs and remarks to entire sections. To help you locate the Maple material appropriate for specific topics, we include below a list pointing to the text sections containing Maple examples and the pages where they occur. Note, however, that this material assumes you are familiar with the basics of start- ing a Maple session, preferably with a graphical user interface, which typically displays the prompt > when it is waiting for your input. In this book the input is shown in red. It normally concludes with a semicolon (;) followed by pressing the key, which we omit from our examples. The output is typically printed by Maple centred in the window; we show it in blue. For instance,

factor(x^2-x-2); .x C 1/.x � 2/ Output can be supressed by using a colon (:) instead of a semicolon at the end of the input. The authors used Maple 10 for preparing the Maple examples in this edition. They should work equally well in later editions. These examples are by no means complete or exhaustive. For a more complete treatment of Maple as a tool for doing calculus, the authors highly recommend the excellent Maple lab manual Calculus: The Maple Way, written by Professor Robert Israel of the University of British Columbia. Like this book, it is published by Pearson Canada.

A-35 A P P E N D I X VI Doing Calculus with Python ” Software is Ephemeral; Mathematics is not! ” Christopher Essex, 1954- Private Communication A computer language called Python has emerged from the open-source software com- munity and developed into a leading tool for data analysis. The full story of this new language is beyond the scope of this text, but its impact stems from the powerful ap- plication libraries written in and for Python. We will consider how the tools that these libraries provide can be used, and not misused, with particular focus on properties that are common to all software when applied to mathematics, always keeping in mind that mathematics software is an application of mathematics, not the reverse. In practice, Python can be used in scientific applications without addressing it at the primitive level. Python is typically employed through a collection of program libraries, which manifest as a collection of commands defined by these libraries. There are a number of packages that are relevant for mathematics applications. We will sample some of the primary ones here. Key commands emerging form the libraries and their syntax will become clear through the examples below. Important relevant Python packages are Numpy, Matplotlib, Scipy, and Sympy. The last of these is where we shall begin. It creates a computer algebra environment, similar to that provided by Maple. Practical mathematics on computers also requires floating-point calculations. That is what Numpy deals with. Matplotlib is the plotting library, which has syntax not unlike Matlab. Scipy gets honourable mention focusing on standard scientific routines. We will not explore it here. It stands in as an exam- ple for an array of specialized packages developed for members of various scientific communities. Finally, we need an interface environment for inputting commands and receiving output. Such environments are independent of Python. We have used Anaconda, which presents a collection of interfaces connected to Python, and it can be installed on all standard platforms quite easily. We have selected the Python 3 version. But given the ephemeral nature of software, this version may be obsolete by the time of reading. That is, of course, not true for the mathematics. Among Anaconda’s program interfaces we selected Jupyter Notebooks. They allow us to proceed with an interpreter-like environment that keeps the focus more on the mathematics than on the Python syntax. The result is similar to the worksheets Maple uses, or indeed any of the other modern interpreter-like environments such as those of Matlab and Mathematica. Running Jupyter notebooks opens your browser to implement the environment, but it does work without the Internet. The environment provides numbered input and output cells labelled “In[n]” and “Out[n].” Each input cell has one or more input lines. A new line in the cell is gen- erated by a simple return or enter. But to generate output or create a new input cell, you can either press Shift-Enter or simply click the Run button at the top of the notebook. Not all input cells produce output. When you select Jupyter Notebook from

Page 1144

A-36 APPENDIX VI Doing Calculus with Python the Anaconda menu, you will get a list of files on your computer. You can select New at the top of the page and create a new Jupyter notebook with filename extension .jpynb. You can save the file in a directory of your choice on your computer, or you may dis- card them if you are just experimenting. But this is invisible while working with the console as an interpreter-like interface. Notebooks can also have formatted commentary between cells. Each Jupyter Notebook starts with a line of option headings: File Edit View Insert Cell Kernel Widgets Help clicking on any of these leads to a list of options. You should review the contents of these lists if you wish to explore Python in detail, but simple explorations can be done without them. Early results in a notebook can affect later ones, so a useful option is to click the Kernel button and select Restart and run all . This results in all the cells being numbered and executed in order from the top down. Sympy and Elementary Algebra We begin by illustrating some of Sympy’s capabilities in doing simple algebraic cal- culations involving sums, differences, products, and quotients of numbers. First, we import everything in Sympy so that the whole package will be available when needed. Note that a single input line can involve several commands separated by commas. Un- like Maple, Python does not use the symbol ” ^” to denote exponentiation. Instead, it uses a pair of asterisks . Thus x3 means x3 in the Python language. Also, note that Sympy treats simple fractions differently in 2 and 3. In 2 they are converted to real decimals, while in 3 they are kept as fractions, having been declared to be rational numbers. Note that Python uses j rather than i to denote the imaginary unit. Calculus with Sympy Calculus with Sympy follows intuitively. It uses standard notation for functions: sin, cos, … for the trigonometric functions and asin, acos, … for their inverses. It uses exp for the exponential function and both ln and log for the natural logarithm. It uses pi for the number , and E for the number e D exp.1/. Here are some examples of limits, including one-sided limits and limits at ˙1 (to enter infinity on an input line, use a pair of lowercase O’s), that is, oo. Then we will progress to differentiation and integration. When necessary, we can convert integer or rational numbers to decimals using either Float(number) or N(number). In either case we can specify the desired precision (number of significant digits) in the number by including a second argument. The default precision is 15. In [ 1 ] from sympy import * In [ 2 ] Float(pi), Float(pi, 6), N(E, 10), N(sqrt(2),4) Out[ 2 ] (3.141592653589793, 3.14159), 2.718281828, 1.414) In [ 3 ] x, y, z, t, u, v, a, b, c = symbols(‘x y z t u v a b c’) The limit( ) command takes three inputs, a function f; a variable x; and a number a at

The terms of the Taylor polynomial for log.x/ (i.e., ln.x/) in powers of x � 1 of order less than 6 are calculated by In [ 33 ] log(x).series(x, 1, 6) Out[ 33 ] x � 1 C .x � 1/2 2 C .x � 1/3 3 � .x � 1/4 4 C .x � 1/5 5 C O�.x � 1/6I x ! 1 In [ 34 ] sqrt(sin(x)).series(x, pi/2, 8) Out[ 34 ] 1 � �x �  2 2 4 C �x �  2 4 96 � 19 �x �  2 6 5760 C O�.x �  2 /8I x !  2  Vector Calculus with Sympy Sympy has a subordinate module sympy.vector for dealing with vectors in 3-space. This module must be imported in addition to Sympy itself. In [ 1 ] from sympy import  In [ 2 ] from sympy.vector import  Much of classical vector calculus is associated with the operator, r. It is a vector with partial derivative operators in terms of variables corresponding to the coordinate axes. From a programming perspective, that requires these special variables to be identified in order to connect them to the operator r. Sympy.vector thus asks us to identify these variables connected to a particular coordinate system. A simple three-dimensional coordinate system is declared. In [ 3 ] C = CoordSys3D(‘C’) This coordinate system is automatically equipped with three coordinate variables (C.x, C.y, C.z) and three unit vectors (C.i, C.j, C.k). These are reserved variables that are the only ones that relate to r. Observe that In [ 4 ] x, y, z = symbols(‘x y z’) In [ 5 ] x == C.x Out[ 5 ] False Thus, Sympy does not see any connection between the character x and the coordinate C.x. The same is true for the other coordinates. This is counterintuitive. Furthermore, if we simply input In [ 6 ] C.x Out[ 6 ] xC The output bold font xC representing C.x would suggest it is a vector by any normal mathematical conventions, but this is computer science, not mathematics. So if you are clear that xC is a scalar, no problems ensue. Similarly for yC and zC . However, be aware that this can be very confusing for novices. No such confusion emerges if the vector components are numerical. For example,

APPENDIX VI Doing Calculus with Python A-43 Mathematical Graphics Using Matplotlib Matplotlib is a Python package with extensive support for producing various kinds of figures for data analysis. Here we will give just a few examples of its use in producing two- and three-dimensional graphs of functions similar to those produced by Maple elsewhere in this book. There are differences. Here we will use the Matplotlib package Pyplot, and instead of the Sympy package, which supports mathematical functions symbolically, we will use here the package Numpy, which is more useful for producing real values for functions. We begin by importing these packages, the whole of Numpy and only the parts of Pyplot that we will actually use. These latter will have to be prefixed with plt. In [ 1 ] from numpy import  In [ 2 ] import matplotlib.pyplot as plt Our first example will be a plot of two graphs, y D cos.x/ sin.20x/ and y D cos.x/. The whole program can be put in just one Jupyter input cell. In [ 3 ] x = linspace(-pi, pi, 200) y = cos(x)sin(20x) plt.plot(x, y, color=‘blue’) y = cos(x) plt.plot(x, y, color=‘red’) plt.text(0.67, 0.86, ‘y=cos(x)’, fontsize=12, color=‘red’) plt.text(0.28, -1.00, ‘y = cos(x)sin(20x)’, fontsize=12, color=‘blue’) plt.text(-4.5, -0.1, ‘y’, fontsize=12) plt.text(-0.5, -1.45, ‘x’, fontsize=12) plt.savefig(‘modulation’) Note that the linspace command determines the x-interval of the plot, and the number of equal subdivisions of that interval used to plot points. The y-interval is determined by the formulas provided for y. All plt.text lines have at least three arguments. The first two are the coordinates of the lower left corner of the text, and the third is the text string itself. Also, the last line in the program displays the plot and saves the figure to a file of a suitable type (e.g., .png, .pdf, : : : .) If we replace that line by one saying “plt.show()” it would just display the plot but not save it to a file.

A-44 APPENDIX VI Doing Calculus with Python Our next example redoes what we did with Maple in Example 11 of Section P.4 on page 31. That is, we attempt to plot the graph y D jx C 1j � 1 x on a very short interval Œ�6  10�16; 4  10�16. Since x C 1 > 0 for all such x, the numerator of the fractions simplifies to .x C 1/ � 1 D x, and so the fraction is actually x=x D 1, except for being undefined at x D 0. We expect to get the line shown in blue on the graph below. However, what we do get is the red curves and the short red horizontal line y D 0 near x D 0. Remark In fact, we could replace jx C 1j with .x C 1/ in the expression for y and we would still get the same graph. Even the parentheses would force x to be added to 1 before 1 was subtracted from the result. In [ 4 ] x = linspace(-6/1016, 5/1016, 200) y = (abs(1+x) - 1)/x plt.plot(x,y, ‘r.’, markersize=5.0) y = x/x plt.plot(x,y, color=‘blue’) plt.text(-5.510**-16, 1.70, ‘y = (|1+x| - 1) / x’, font- size=12, color=‘red’) plt.text(0.010**-16, 0.8, ‘y D 1’, fontsize=12, color=‘blue’) plt.text(0.010**-16, 0.1, ‘y D 0’, fontsize=12, color=‘red’) plt.text(-0.0810**-16, -0.40, ‘x’, fontsize=12) plt.text(-8.5*10**-16, 0.98, ‘y’, fontsize=12) plt.savefig(‘badalgebra’) How could both Python and Maple get it so wrong? The answer, as pointed out in Section P.4, is that computers are very finite devices that can only store finitely many numbers, and a number can be stored correctly only if it has a limited number of significant binary digits. For values of x close to zero, the significant binary digits of 1 C x must include the 1 and all the zeros between 1 and all those of x. This is not possible for x very close to zero. The red arcs correspond to intervals where a binary significant digit remains until eventually it and all other significant digits of x are lost

Page 1153

APPENDIX VI Doing Calculus with Python A-45 and the computer stores 1 for 1 C x. Then the fraction becomes 0=x D 0. If the numerator had been 1 C x � 1 the program would likely have simplified the numerator to x and the fraction to 1, giving the blue line. However, as pointed out in the above remark, even ..1 C x/ � 1/=x would give the same result as .j1 C xj � 1/=x. For our final example, we will plot a two-dimensional surface in 3-space, specifi- cally the “monkey saddle” with equation z D x3 � 3xy2. This will require, in addition to Pyplot and Numpy, a special toolkit from Matplotlib called mplot3d. In [ 5 ] from mpl_toolkits import mplot3d x = linspace(-2, 2, 20) y = linspace(-2, 2, 20) x, y = meshgrid(x, y) ax = plt.axes(projection=‘3d’) def f(x, y): return x3 - 3xy2 z = f(x, y) ax.plot_surface(x, y, z, cmap=‘viridis’) ax.set_xlabel(‘x’) ax.set_ylabel(‘y’) ax.set_zlabel(‘z’) ax.set_xticks([-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]) ax.set_yticks([-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]) ax.set_zticks([-15, -10, -5, 0, 5, 10, 15]) plt.savefig(‘monkeysaddle’)
